drills.title: Program against an interface
drills.prompt: Arrange the lines into an alert program: an interface Notifier, a class Email that implements it, and a main that calls it through the interface type. The first class must hold main. Interface and Email can go in either order. Two lines do not belong.
drills.explain: A class implements an interface with implements (extends is for a parent class). Interface methods are automatically public, so the implementing method must say public too: a plain String send(...) would be rejected for "weaker access privileges". The variable has the interface type, so main does not care which notifier it really is.

drills.title: Switch over a sealed type
drills.prompt: Fill the blanks so the receipt method handles both payment types without a default branch, and the program prints the goal output.
code: record Upi(int amount, String handle) implements Payment {}
drills.explain: A sealed interface lists the only types allowed to implement it (permits), so the compiler knows the switch covers every case and no default is needed. A record gets accessor methods named after its components, so it is u.handle(), not getHandle(). If you add a third payment type, this switch stops compiling until you handle it.

drills.title: Which pay() runs?
drills.prompt: Read the code and type exactly what it prints, one line per line of output.
code: Employee(String name, int salary) { this.name = name; this.salary = salary; }
Manager(String name, int salary, int bonus) { super(name, salary); this.bonus = bonus; }
drills.explain: ravi is declared as an Employee but the object is a Manager, and Java runs the pay() of the real object. describe() is only written in Employee, yet the call to pay() inside it still reaches Manager.pay(), so Ravi shows 100000. instanceof also looks at the real object: true for ravi, false for asha.

drills.title: Weaker access
drills.prompt: This program does not compile. Click the line the compiler complains about, then choose the fix.
drills.explain: Every method in an interface is public, and an implementing method may not be less visible than the one it implements. Without a modifier the method is package-private, which is weaker, so the compiler refuses. protected and private are weaker too, and static would make it a different kind of method.

drills.title: Review the AI's checkout code
drills.prompt: An AI assistant wrote this checkout code. It compiles and runs, but tick the real problems (there are two).
code: sealed interface Payment permits Cash, Upi {}
record Upi(int amount, String handle) implements Payment {}

issues.text: The switch has a default branch even though Payment is sealed
issues.why: Without default the compiler proves every payment type is handled, and it stops compiling the day someone adds Card. With default the new type silently prints Other.

issues.text: fee uses an instanceof chain that ends in a catch-all return 0
issues.why: A new payment type would get fee 0 without any warning. A switch over the sealed type (or a method on Payment itself) lets the compiler flag the missing case.

non_issues.text: The records need getAmount() and getHandle() methods
non_issues.why: A record creates accessors named after its components: c.amount() and u.handle(). Writing getters would only add noise.

non_issues.text: Payment has no methods, so it should be an abstract class
non_issues.why: A sealed interface with no methods is a normal way to say "these are the only variants". The records cannot extend a class anyway, since they already extend Record.

non_issues.text: case Cash c needs a cast before c.amount() can be used
non_issues.why: A pattern case names the variable with the right type already, so no cast is needed.

drills.explain: When a type family is sealed, let the compiler check it: no default in the switch, and no instanceof ladders with a silent fallback. Adding a new case then becomes a compile error you can fix, not a quiet bug.
